newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro Disney to show second annual profit.
newsitem.headline: Euro Disney to show second annual profit.

text.p: Euro Disney is pulling out all the stops as it prepares to mark its fifth anniversary in 1997 -- a milestone many critics did not expect the theme park operator to celebrate.

Four years after a rocky start, Euro Disney is expected to confirm next month that its recovery is on track and its Disneyland Paris theme park a success by reporting a second consecutive annual profit.
Analysts predict the company will report a net profit for the year ended on Sept. 30 of between 160 million and 200 million francs ($31 million to $39 million) on Nov. 14 when its results are due.

After losing more than 7 billion francs ($1.4 billion) in its first two years, Euro Disney emerged from the red for the first time last year when it reported a net profit of 114 million francs ($22 million) and a 21 percent jump in attendance to 10.7 million people.
Excluding an extraordinary gain from the repurchase of convertible bonds, its 1994/95 profit was 2 million francs ($388,000).
Euro Disney Chairman Philippe Bourguignon said last month the company should "do better this year" after a "satisfying" summer season.
"The company is now at cruising speed and delivering operating cash flow, and the theme park is drawing crowds," a spokesman said last week.

Its performance has refuted doubters who said the Disney concept would flop in France, but the stocks is still worth only a fraction of its 1992 high above 160 francs ($31). It was trading at 10.80 francs ($2.10) on Tuesday.

Analyst Jacques Falzon at brokerage Transbourse expects Euro Disney to show a profit of 200 million francs ($39 million) -- on the high end of expectations -- but is wary of the stock. "It's very speculative. I don't recommend it based on the fundamentals."
Analysts say the theme park operator is weighed down by the costs of a 1994 six billion franc ($1.16 billion) financial restructuring.
The deal pulled the company from the brink of failure and provided a brief debt holiday that allowed it to emerge from its losses, but the debt costs are being gradually phased in.

Although 1997 marks the fifth anniversary, which will be celebrated with customary Disney flare, including the unveiling of a new castle in January and a springtime festival, it will be a difficult year because of the rising charges.
From 1998/99, royalties and management fees to 39 percent U.S. owner The Walt Disney Co. also will be reinstated.
"They're having to run just to stand still," said analyst Nigel Reed at Paribas Capital Markets. "It's like being on a down escalator when you're trying to go up."
Analysts will be scrutinising attendance, hotel occupancy, and costs when the results are issued to gauge the company's prospects in a weak consumer spending climate in France.

Some suspect Euro Disney may have to seek a second debt restructuring, particularly if it has to sink money into its ambitious Phase II project which includes a 108,000 square foot shopping complex adjacent to the theme park in the Paris suburb of Marne-la-Vallee.
